content.text:
Amgen’s main distinction is that it combines **biotech-style drug discovery with the scale and infrastructure of a large pharmaceutical company**. That combination isn’t unique to Amgen, but it’s a defining feature of the company.

- **A long biotech track record:** Founded in 1980, Amgen was among the companies that helped establish modern biotechnology. It still emphasizes understanding disease biology and using human genetic data and newer technologies to find drug targets. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/about?utm_source=openai))
- **In-house capabilities across the medicine-making process:** Amgen works across discovery, development, manufacturing, and global delivery. Its biologics manufacturing experience is especially important because medicines made using living cells can be technically complex to produce reliably. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/science/manufacturing?utm_source=openai))
- **A broad mix of medicines and business lines:** It works across general medicine, rare diseases, inflammation, and oncology—and sells both innovative medicines and biosimilars. In 2025, biosimilars generated $3.0 billion in sales, according to the company’s annual report. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/about?utm_source=openai))
- **Big-company reach:** Amgen has the ability to run large clinical programs and supply medicines internationally, unlike many smaller biotech firms that depend on partners for parts of development or manufacturing. The company reports a presence in about 100 countries. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/about?utm_source=openai))

**In short:** Amgen is a mature, globally scaled biotech with deep biologics and manufacturing expertise—not a small research-focused startup, and not simply a traditional pharmaceutical company. Those strengths come with the usual large-company trade-off: it has more resources and reach, but its priorities span a wider portfolio than a specialist biotech’s.
